text.p: These are the leading stories in the Malawian press on Wednesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Lawyers representing Malawi's main opposition Malawi Congress Party (MCP) on Tuesday rejected the presence of two foreign lawyers in an appeal case for a High Court ruling against government earlier this year. Defence lawyer Temwa Nyirenda told the Supreme Court in Blantyre that two British lawyers, Patrick Elias and Andrew Dobson, hired by the Malawi government were contrary to the constitution because they were not public servants. The government is fighting against the High Court ruling that Parliament's bill, mandating it to take away former President Kamuzu Banda's Press Trust that controls the country's 40 percent economy, was null and void.

- The Malawi government has described as distortion of facts British High Commisioner John Martin's claim two weeks ago that government overspent 300-million Malawi kwacha ($20-million) in the first quarter of the budget.
- Long queues of taxi operators boycotting car parks are causing traffic jams in Lilongwe, the Malawi capital, in protest against parking fees of up to 10 Malawi kwacha per day.

- Parliament, scheduled to meet on October 22, will not sit next week due to the absence of the opposition parties who boycotted the last proceedings. Government announced recently parliament would still meet with or without the opposition.

- Malawi's former second vice president and president for opposition Alliance for Democracy (AFORD) Chakufwa Chihana has challenged government to take him to court for defying a loan repayment order of 350,000 Malawi kwacha ($23,000) saying it was in bad taste.

- An international book publishing firm, Macmillan Malawi Limited, has threatened to close its offices in the country, barely a year after its opening, due to insecurity. General Manager Lorraine Dunk said her firm has experienced a spate of robberies and was ransacked last Friday and lost 40,000 Malawi kwacha worth of goods.
